title: LED + resistor
hint: Build the trainer, move the jumper, predict the current and read the meter, then break it on purpose
overview: The first circuit of the course has no chip at all: 5 V, a switch, one resistor and a red LED, with a multimeter in the loop to read the current. A jumper picks the resistor: 220 Ω, 1 kΩ, 10 kΩ or a bare wire. Work out each current on paper first, I = (V − V_F) / R with about 2 V across the LED, then move the jumper and check the meter: 13.6, 3.0 and 0.30 mA. Then break it on purpose: no resistor, the LED or the capacitor in backwards, a missing USB-C pull-down, a cold joint, swapped supply leads, 12 V instead of 5 V, a supply that runs out of current. Every LED, pull-up and sensor divider on a robot runs on this one formula.

power.label: Plug in the USB-C charger
power.ok: Powered: the LED is lit and the meter reads its current

J1.name: USB-C power jack
J1.what: A power-only USB-C receptacle: VBUS, GND and the two CC pins, no data. The charger's 5 V comes in here.

J2.name: Screw terminal for a bench supply
J2.what: Two-way 5.08 mm screw terminal: red lead to +, black to −. Nothing on the board stops a swapped pair, on purpose.

R4.name: 5.1 kΩ CC1 pull-down
R4.what: A USB-C charger keeps its 5 V off until it sees 5.1 kΩ from a CC pin to ground: that is how it knows a device, not a loose cable end, is plugged in. R4 sits on CC1.

R5.name: 5.1 kΩ CC2 pull-down
R5.what: The same 5.1 kΩ on CC2. A USB-C plug fits either way up and only one CC pin connects at a time, so each needs its own.

SW1.name: Slide switch
SW1.what: Breaks the 5 V line right after the supply, where a robot's power switch goes. Slide it to ON.

C1.name: 100 µF 16 V electrolytic capacitor
C1.what: Smooths the moment you plug in. It is polarised: the stripe on the sleeve marks the − lead, which goes toward GND. Reverse-biased, an electrolytic leaks, heats and vents.

R1.name: 220 Ω resistor
R1.what: Red, red, brown, gold: 22 × 10 = 220 Ω, ±5 %. (5 V − 2 V) / 220 Ω = 13.6 mA, bright and well under the LED's 30 mA.

R2.name: 1 kΩ resistor
R2.what: Brown, black, red, gold: 10 × 100 = 1 kΩ. 3 V / 1000 Ω = 3.0 mA: clearly lit, a usual indicator current.

R3.name: 10 kΩ resistor
R3.what: Brown, black, orange, gold: 10 × 1000 = 10 kΩ. 0.30 mA: dim but visible. 10 kΩ is also the classic pull-up value.

JL1.name: Wire link (no resistor)
JL1.what: A bare wire, 0 Ω: the NONE row. Here only the LED itself and the supply limit the current. Try it once, on purpose.

JP1.name: 2 × 4 jumper header
JP1.what: Each row joins one resistor to the LED's anode while the jumper cap sits on it. Two caps at once put two resistors in parallel.

SHUNT.name: Jumper cap
SHUNT.what: Joins the two pins of one JP1 row. Moving it is how you change the resistor.

D1.name: Red 5 mm LED
D1.what: A red 5 mm LED (WP7113ID class): about 2 V across it when lit (1.9 V typical at 10 mA), 30 mA DC at most. Current flows one way only, from the long leg (anode) to the leg by the flat on the rim (cathode).

TP1.name: Test point (+)
TP1.what: The meter's red lead clips on here. The current comes from the supply to TP1, goes through the meter and comes back on TP2.

TP2.name: Test point (COM)
TP2.what: The meter's black lead (COM). From here the current goes on through the resistor the jumper picks and the LED, to ground.

MM1.name: Pocket multimeter, 200 mA range
MM1.what: On its 200 mA DC range with the red lead in the mA jack. It sits in series, so all the LED's current goes through it: it reads the loop current. Above 200 mA it shows OL.

math.vf: a red LED drops about 2 V when lit
math.watts: heat in the resistor (a 1/4 W part)
math.led: heat in the LED (75 mW at most)

code.what: Jumper on 220 Ω: Ohm's law for the LED, I = (V - V_F) / R
code.verdict: 13.6 mA: bright and safe. Run a 5 mm red LED at 5-20 mA, never above 30 mA
3.0 mA: clearly lit, an indicator's current

code.what: Jumper on NONE: the bare wire link
code.bands: the wire link: no resistor at all
code.nothing: no answer, nothing in the formula limits the current
code.real: the real limit is the LED's own few ohms and the charger: hundreds of mA
code.verdict: ten times the LED's 30 mA maximum: it burns out

unplug.title: Unplug it
unplug.body: The trainer comes plugged in, its LED lit at 220 Ω. Unplug the USB-C cable before you touch a part: never work on a live board.

strip.title: Strip it to the bare PCB
strip.body: Take every part off, the jumper cap and the meter too. What is left is the board: copper, solder mask and the silkscreen that says where each part goes.
strip.refusal: Unplug the power first: never work on a live board

low.title: Fit the low parts
low.body: Through-hole parts go in from the lowest to the tallest, so each one lies flat while you solder it: the three resistors and the wire link, the two CC pull-downs, the slide switch, the two test points and the jumper header.
low.refusal: Strip the board first, with the power off

tall.title: Fit the tall parts
tall.body: Now the USB-C jack, the screw terminal, C1 and the LED. Two of them only fit one way: D1's long leg (anode) goes in the + hole, and C1's striped lead (−) goes toward GND, as the silkscreen shows.
tall.refusal: Low parts first: a tall part in the way keeps the low ones from lying flat

solder.title: Solder every joint
solder.body: Heat the pad and the lead together, then feed in the solder: a good joint is a shiny little cone. A dull, grainy blob is a cold joint, and it only makes contact some of the time.

jumper-meter.title: Jumper cap and meter
jumper-meter.body: Put the jumper cap on the 220 row, then clip the meter's red lead to TP1 and its black lead to TP2. The meter closes the loop: without it no current flows at all.
jumper-meter.refusal: Solder everything first: the cap and the meter go on last

plug.title: Predict, then plug in
plug.body: Work it out before you plug in: the LED takes about 2 V, so the resistor gets 3 V, and 3 V / 220 Ω = 13.6 mA. Plug the charger in: the LED lights and the meter reads 13.6.

row-1k.title: Move the jumper to 1 kΩ
row-1k.body: About five times the resistance, about a fifth of the current: 3 V / 1000 Ω = 3.0 mA, and the LED is plainly dimmer. At this current a real red LED drops nearer 1.8 V, so a real meter shows 3.0 to 3.2 mA.

row-10k.title: Move it to 10 kΩ
row-10k.body: Ten times more again: 0.30 mA. The LED is dim but still visible, and the resistor warms by less than a milliwatt.

row-220.title: Back to 220 Ω
row-220.body: 13.6 mA again. Every reading matched the sum: that is Ohm's law, I = V / R, where V is the 3 V the resistor gets after the LED takes its 2 V.

no-resistor.title: Break it: no resistor
no-resistor.body: Move the jumper to NONE, so only the bare wire link sits between the supply and the LED. Watch the LED and the meter. Then repair it: unplug, move the jumper back to 220 Ω and fit a new LED.

led-backwards.title: Break it: the LED in backwards
led-backwards.body: Fit D1 the wrong way round and power up. Then turn it round and power up again.

cap-backwards.title: Break it: C1 in backwards
cap-backwards.body: Fit C1 with its stripe toward + and power up. Then fit a new one the right way round.

cc-missing.title: Break it: leave out R4
cc-missing.body: Build the board without one of the two 5.1 kΩ CC pull-downs and plug the charger in. Then fit R4 and plug in again.

cold-led.title: Break it: a cold joint on the LED
cold-led.body: One of D1's joints is dull and grainy. Watch the LED and the meter, then reheat the joint.

reverse-supply.title: Break it: swap the bench supply's leads
reverse-supply.body: Power the board from the bench supply on J2 with red and black swapped. Then swap them back and fit a new C1.

over-voltage.title: Break it: 12 V on the 5 V input
over-voltage.body: Turn the bench supply up to 12 V. Read the meter, then wait a few seconds. Repair it with the supply back at 5 V and a new LED.

current-limit.title: Break it: a 10 mA current limit
current-limit.body: Set the bench supply's current limit to 10 mA, less than the LED wants. Read the meter and the supply voltage, then raise the limit again.

usb-again.title: Back on USB
usb-again.body: Plug the charger back in. The meter reads 13.6 mA: the trainer is whole again.

no-resistor.title: No resistor (jumper on NONE)
no-resistor.symptom: A bright flash and OL on the meter, then the LED is dark for good and the meter reads 0.
no-resistor.explanation: With 0 Ω in the row, nothing in I = (V − V_F) / R limits the current. Only the LED's own few ohms and the charger's limit hold it back: hundreds of milliamps against the LED's 30 mA maximum. The die and its bond wire overheat in a moment and the LED goes open.
no-resistor.fix: Unplug, move the jumper back to 220 Ω and fit a new LED: a burnt LED never comes back.

led-backwards.title: LED in backwards
led-backwards.symptom: The LED stays dark and the meter reads 0.00.
led-backwards.explanation: An LED conducts only from anode to cathode. Turned round it is reverse-biased, and at 5 V (its reverse rating) only a few microamps of leakage flow. It survives; it just stays dark.
led-backwards.fix: Unplug and turn D1 round: the long leg (anode) in the + hole, the flat side toward −.

cap-backwards.title: C1 in backwards
cap-backwards.symptom: C1 hisses and its vent opens. The LED keeps working.
cap-backwards.explanation: An aluminium electrolytic blocks current one way only. Reverse-biased it leaks more and more, heats up, makes gas and the scored vent on top opens. The LED doesn't need C1, so it stays lit, but the capacitor is ruined.
cap-backwards.fix: Unplug and fit a new C1 with its stripe (−) toward GND.

cc-missing.title: R4 left out (a USB-C pull-down)
cc-missing.symptom: Nothing at all: the LED is dark and the meter reads 0, as if the charger were dead.
cc-missing.explanation: A USB-C charger keeps its 5 V off until it sees a 5.1 kΩ pull-down on the CC pin, so a loose cable end is never live. R4 and R5 are those pull-downs, one for each way up of the plug, and without R4 this way up gets no power. A USB-A-to-C cable always gives 5 V, which hides the mistake until someone uses a C-to-C cable.
cc-missing.fix: Unplug, fit R4 (5.1 kΩ) and solder it.

cold-led.title: Cold joint on D1
cold-led.symptom: The LED flickers and the meter jumps between 13.6 and 0.
cold-led.explanation: A cold joint is solder that never wetted the pad properly: dull, grainy, sometimes cracked. It touches, then it doesn't, so the loop opens and closes. On a robot this is the fault that comes and goes when it moves.
cold-led.fix: Unplug and reheat the joint with a little fresh solder until it flows into a shiny cone.

reverse-supply.title: Bench supply leads swapped
reverse-supply.symptom: The LED stays dark, then C1 vents.
reverse-supply.explanation: J2 has no reverse-polarity diode, on purpose: one would eat 0.7 V of the 3 V this lesson is about. With the leads swapped, the 5 V line sits at −5 V. The LED is reverse-biased and simply blocks, but C1, right across the supply, is reverse-biased too, and vents.
reverse-supply.fix: Unplug, swap the leads (red to +), then fit a new C1.

over-voltage.title: 12 V on the 5 V input
over-voltage.symptom: The LED glares and the meter reads 45.5 mA. A few seconds later it flashes and goes dark.
over-voltage.explanation: (12 V − 2 V) / 220 Ω = 45 mA, half as much again as the LED's 30 mA maximum, and 0.45 W in a 1/4 W resistor. The simulator burns the LED out after about 3 s; a real one may last longer, getting dimmer as it dies. Either way the resistor was sized for 5 V, not 12.
over-voltage.fix: Unplug, set the supply back to 5 V (or work out a bigger resistor for 12 V) and fit a new LED.

current-limit.title: Supply current limit at 10 mA
current-limit.symptom: The LED is a little dimmer, the meter reads 10.0 and the supply sags to 4.2 V.
current-limit.explanation: A bench supply holds its voltage only until the load wants more than its current limit. Then it lowers the voltage to hold the current at the limit: 10 mA here, which leaves 2 V + 10 mA × 220 Ω = 4.2 V. That is a brown-out: nothing breaks, but the circuit no longer gets what you set.
current-limit.fix: Raise the current limit above what the circuit needs (20 mA is plenty here), or use a bigger resistor.

current.led: The LED loop, as the meter reads it

ohms-law.title: Ohm's law in a sketch
ohms-law.brief: Make an Uno do the paper maths and print the current for each jumper row (220, 1000 and 10000 ohm) with a 5 V supply and a 2 V LED, in the form "220 ohm: 13.64 mA". The starter prints 0 mA for all three rows: find out why. Then add one line with the smallest resistor that keeps the LED at 20 mA: "20 mA needs 150 ohm".

hints.1: In C++ an int divided by an int is an int: 3 / 220 is 0, and 0 × 1000 is still 0.
hints.2: Make the numbers float (5.0, 2.0, 1000.0) and the division keeps its decimals.
hints.3: R = (V − V_F) / I, with I in amps: 3.0 / 0.020 = 150. Serial.print(x, 0) prints a float with no decimals.

code.starter: Ohm's law on an Uno: the current for each jumper row
code.law: I = (V - V_F) / R, times 1000 for mA
code.smallest: the smallest resistor for 20 mA: R = (V - V_F) / I

pwm-current.title: Set the average current with PWM
pwm-current.brief: Wire the trainer's 220 Ω and LED to pin 9 of an Uno: pin 9, then the resistor, then the LED, then GND. Fully on, pin 9 sits at about 5 V, so the LED draws 13.6 mA. PWM switches the pin fully on and fully off about 490 times a second, so the average current is the duty times 13.6 mA, and that average is what the meter shows. Step the LED through 13.6, 6.8 and 3.4 mA on average, one second each, and print each step.

hints.1: digitalWrite() knows only HIGH and LOW: the full 13.6 mA or nothing.
hints.2: analogWrite(9, duty), with duty from 0 to 255, sets the share of each cycle the pin is on: 128 is about half.

checks.2: The full 13.6 mA in the first second
checks.3: About half, 6.8 mA, in the second
checks.4: About a quarter, 3.4 mA, in the third

code.starter: Three currents with digitalWrite(): it only does full or nothing
code.half: half the current? digitalWrite has only HIGH and LOW
code.peak: the current while the pin is on: (5 - 2) / 220 A
code.duty: the share of each cycle the pin is on, 0-255

led-legs.q: Which way round does D1 go in?

options.1: The flat side of the rim in the + hole
options.2: The long leg (anode) in the + hole
options.3: Either way: an LED works like a resistor

led-legs.why: Current flows from anode to cathode only. The anode is the longer leg; the cathode is the one by the flat on the rim. Backwards, the LED just stays dark.

cap-stripe.q: What does the stripe on C1's sleeve mark?

options.1: The − lead, which goes toward GND

cap-stripe.why: Electrolytics are marked on the negative side. Reverse-biased they leak, heat and vent, so the stripe goes toward GND.

predict.q: A 5 V supply, a red LED that drops about 2 V, and 220 Ω. What will the meter read?
predict.why: The resistor only gets what the LED leaves: 5 V − 2 V = 3 V, and 3 V / 220 Ω = 13.6 mA. 5 V / 220 Ω = 22.7 mA forgets the LED's drop.

series.q: Why does the meter sit between TP1 and TP2, inside the loop?

options.1: So it can measure the supply voltage
options.2: On its mA range a meter can go anywhere
options.3: A current meter has to carry the current it measures, so it goes in series

series.why: On its mA range a meter is nearly a short: a shunt of an ohm or so. In series it reads the loop's current; put across the supply it would short it and blow its fuse.

heat.q: At 10 kΩ the meter reads 0.30 mA. How much heat is in the resistor?
heat.why: P = I² × R = 0.0003² × 10000 = 0.0009 W, under a milliwatt. Even the 220 Ω row makes only 40.9 mW, a sixth of its 1/4 W rating.

pull-up.q: Where else will you meet a 10 kΩ resistor?

options.2: As a fuse in a power line
options.3: As the pull-up or pull-down on a button input

pull-up.why: 10 kΩ lets so little through (0.5 mA at 5 V) that it can hold an input at a level without wasting power. That makes it the classic pull-up.

why.q: Why did the LED die on the NONE row?

options.1: The jumper shorted 5 V straight to GND
options.2: Nothing limited the current: hundreds of mA against a 30 mA maximum
options.3: 5 V is too high a voltage for any LED

why.why: The LED was still in the loop, so it was no dead short, but with 0 Ω only its own few ohms and the charger held the current back. 5 V is fine for an LED with a resistor: the resistor is what sets the current.

ol.q: The meter flashed OL. What did that mean?

options.1: The current was over its 200 mA range

ol.why: OL means over limit: more than the range can show. Swapped leads show a minus sign instead. On a cheap meter a surge like this can also blow the mA fuse.

r330.q: You fit a 330 Ω resistor (orange, orange, brown) instead. What current flows?
r330.why: (5 − 2) V / 330 Ω = 9.1 mA: a little dimmer than 220 Ω, still well lit.

smallest.q: What is the smallest safe resistor for this LED on USB? Allow for USB at 5.25 V, a V_F as low as 1.8 V and the 30 mA maximum.
smallest.why: (5.25 − 1.8) V / 0.030 A = 115 Ω, and the next standard (E12) value up is 120 Ω. 100 Ω would allow 34.5 mA. 220 Ω is safe, but it isn't the smallest.

cc.q: Why do R4 and R5 (5.1 kΩ) sit on the USB-C jack's CC pins?

options.2: A USB-C charger turns its 5 V on only when it sees them

cc.why: The pull-downs tell the charger a device is attached. Without them a C-to-C cable gives no power at all.

two-caps.q: Two jumper caps at once, on the 220 Ω and the 1 kΩ rows. What does the meter read?

options.2: 16.6 mA: the two in parallel make 180 Ω
options.3: 13.6 mA: only the first cap counts

two-caps.why: Both rows join the same two points, so the resistors are in parallel: 220 × 1000 / 1220 = 180 Ω, and 3 V / 180 Ω = 16.6 mA.
